name: Omar Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Omar, and thank you for your time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal working week like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's split in two. I farm 45 hectares of my own, beef cattle and spring barley, and three days a week I work for the Fieldings on their big pig and cereal unit down the valley. At Fieldings' I wash out pens, move pigs, help with the feed system and drive the combine at harvest. At home I do the cattle before and after, and my wife Claire does our books and two other farms' books for a bit of cash.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about that, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good is that I've got my own land and a wage, so one carries the other. Hard is that the wage from Fieldings' is what actually pays the mortgage, and old Mr Fielding keeps talking about selling up. Claire also does dinners at the primary school, and we've still less than a month put by. I use the AI on my phone now and then; my son Lucas showed me how to ask it about cattle movement forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, a bit of sense at last. People should get on with honest work and stop waiting for a machine to save them. I'd say it after church to the other farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it makes no difference to my real worry, which is Mr Fielding selling the unit. If a big company buys it, they'll bring their own staff or their own systems. My wage from the pig unit is the mortgage, and old Mr Fielding (his boss) keeps talking about selling up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working both jobs and do them well, so whoever owns Fieldings' wants to keep me. I'd sell a few beef boxes direct to people in the village to bring in extra. And I'd put the beef box money into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady but worried. The same worry I've had since Mr Fielding turned seventy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the Fieldings did sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go round the other farms asking for work, but there isn't much near here. I might end up driving forty minutes each way to a job. That's diesel we haven't got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Claire think about the beef boxes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Claire says she'll do the orders if I do the butcher runs. She's better at selling than me. She'd have the village signed up in a week.

say: People should get on with **honest work** and not wait for machines.
I'd say it **after church** to the other farmers.
think: My real worry is **Mr Fielding selling** the pig unit.
**Three days' wages** pays the mortgage, simple as that.
do: Work both jobs well so any **new owner keeps him**.
Sell **beef boxes** direct to the village.
Put the beef box money into **savings**.
feel: **Steady but worried**, the same worry since his boss turned seventy.
S0.quote: My wage from the pig unit is the mortgage, and old Mr Fielding (his boss) keeps talking about selling up.
fieldNote: His real risk is a **farm sale**, not AI.
**Few local jobs** would mean long, costly commutes.
His wife Claire is the **better seller** and would run the boxes.

steps.text: Keep working three days a week at the Fielding pig unit
Sell beef boxes direct to families in the village
Bank all beef box money as savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the farms will be all right, but office folk will have a hard time. I'd say young people should get apprenticeships in trades rather than degrees. I'd say it plainly, at church and at the mart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's Claire's bookkeeping that worries me. Two farms pay my wife to do their accounts, and that's exactly what AI takes. The pig unit will get smarter feed software, and I'd need to keep up with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the Fieldings' manager to show me the new feed software properly, so I'm the one who can run it. I'd encourage Claire to take more hours at the school kitchen, which is hands-on. And I'd keep the beef boxes going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for Claire. I'd keep my head and do what's needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Claire feel about losing the bookkeeping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Claire would be upset, because she's proud of it. She did a course in it before the kids. But she's practical; she'd move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI now and then. Would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it more, once I saw it worked on the pig unit. I'm not first in line, but I'm not last either. Lucas would laugh at me.

say: Farms will be all right, but **office folk** will have a hard time.
Young people should get **trade apprenticeships**, not degrees.
think: Claire's **bookkeeping** for two farms is exactly what AI takes.
The pig unit will get **smarter feed software**, and I must keep up.
do: Ask the manager to teach him the **feed software**.
Encourage Claire to take more **school kitchen hours**.
S1.quote: Two farms pay my wife to do their accounts, and that's exactly what AI takes.
fieldNote: The household's exposed income is **Claire's bookkeeping**.
He'd learn the **pig unit software** to protect his wage.
He backs **apprenticeships** over degrees and sees office workers as the ones in trouble.

steps.text: Learn to run the Fielding unit's new feed software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and churches will have to carry each other through this. I'd say the government should keep out of the way and let people adapt. I'd vote for whoever promised to keep farms in family hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, 2028 takes Claire's bookkeeping straight away. By 2031 the robots arrive. A pig unit is the easiest place in farming to put robots: indoor pens, feed systems, cleaning. My three days would be gone, and with it the mortgage money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start building up our own beef herd from 30 to 45 cows, so the home farm can carry more. I'd cut everything else: no new car, no holidays, Lucas's football club only if it's cheap. I'd ask the church's farming group about sharing machinery to cut costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm a calm man, but I'd lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lucas about his future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son to learn a trade with his hands and his head, like an electrician or a machinery fitter. Robots will need fixing. I'd want him close to home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government should keep out. Would you take help if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was a loan or a grant to build up the farm, yes. Not money for nothing. I've never taken a handout and I'd rather not start.

say: Families and **churches** will have to carry each other through this.
Government should **keep out** of the way and let people adapt.
think: AGI in 2028 takes **Claire's bookkeeping** straight away.
By 2031, **robots** in the pig unit take my three days and the mortgage money.
do: Build the beef herd from **30 to 45 cows**.
Cut out **car, holidays** and costly clubs.
Share machinery through the **church farming group**.
S2.quote: A pig unit is the easiest place in farming to put robots: indoor pens, feed systems, cleaning.
fieldNote: He sees **indoor pig work** as the first hands-on job robots take.
He'd **expand his own herd** rather than look for wage work.
He'd take a **loan or grant**, never money for nothing.

steps.text: Grow the home beef herd from 30 to 45 cows
Drop holidays and the new car, and keep only cheap clubs
Share machinery through the church farming group
Vote for the party backing family-owned farms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time enough for anyone willing to work. I'd say apprenticeships should be offered in every village. I'd say it at the church council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, robots around 2034 give me time to grow the home farm slowly and pay down some of the mortgage. Claire would lose the books by 2031, but she'd have time to switch. I can see my way through this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the herd by three or four cows a year. I'd get Lucas an apprenticeship with a machinery dealer at sixteen. And I'd ask Fieldings' to train me on any robots they buy, so I stay useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. Five years of warning feels like a long winter you know you'll get through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the Fieldings sell during those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go home full time sooner. With a bigger herd, the home farm could almost carry us. Almost is the word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your faith fit into all of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It keeps me from panicking. I believe we're meant to work and to look after each other. The robots don't change that.

say: Five years is **time enough** for anyone willing to work.
Every village should be offered **apprenticeships**, starting now.
think: Robots around 2034 give me time to **grow the home farm**.
Claire loses the books by 2031, but has **time to switch**.
do: Grow the herd by **three or four cows** a year.
Get Lucas an **apprenticeship** at a machinery dealer.
Ask to be **trained on robots** at the pig unit.
feel: **Anxious but steady**, like a long winter he'll get through.
S3.quote: Five years of warning feels like a long winter you know you'll get through.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **grow his own herd** instead of rushing.
He'd stay useful by **training on robots** at his employer's unit.

steps.text: Add three or four beef cows to the home herd each year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and people should use it. I'd say farm families should prepare their children. I'd say it calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots in 2039 mean I'd be 56, and the kids would be grown. The worry about the sale is still there all the way through. Mr Fielding (his boss) selling the pig unit is my real clock, not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep both jobs going and grow the herd slowly. I'd pay off a bit more of the mortgage each year. I'd help Lucas and Amélie think about trades or college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with the old worry. I'd sleep fine most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Mr Fielding sold in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to rent some of his land if the new owner didn't want it. That could make the home farm big enough to live on. Every problem has a corner of opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change about how you use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn a bit more each year, slowly. Lucas could teach me on Sunday afternoons. It'd do us both good.

Farm families should **prepare their children** in good time.
think: Robots in 2039 come when I'm 56 and **the kids are grown**.
Mr Fielding selling is **my real clock**, not the robots.
do: Keep **both jobs** and grow the herd slowly.
Pay off **more of the mortgage** each year.
Help Lucas and Amélie weigh **trades or college**.
feel: **Uneasy** with the old worry, but **sleeping fine** most nights.
S4.quote: Mr Fielding (his boss) selling the pig unit is my real clock, not the robots.
fieldNote: Ten years puts the focus back on **his employer's sale**.
He sees a **chance to rent land** if the unit is sold.
Sunday lessons with **his son** are his way into AI.

steps.text: Keep working at the Fielding unit and the home farm

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Claire's books go first and then my wage at the pig unit, and the home farm can't carry us yet. What would help is apprenticeships for the young, and cheap loans for small farmers to grow their own herds. Not handouts, just a fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what work means to a man. It's not just money, it's getting up for something. I'd rather be poor and useful than comfortable and idle.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be poor and useful than comfortable and idle.
portrait: Omar, 43, farms **45 hectares** of beef and barley and works three days on a big pig unit.
The **pig unit wage** pays the mortgage, and his elderly boss keeps talking about selling.
His wife Claire's **bookkeeping** for two farms is the household's most AI-exposed income.
A churchgoer who prefers **apprenticeships and loans** to handouts, he uses AI now and then.
He's **anxious** in most worlds and **alarmed** if robots reach pig units by 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Claire's books and then his pig unit wage would both go.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** for the young and **cheap loans** to grow their own herds.
